Maladaptive Strategies.value: go over and over why the event happened to me
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma

vignette:
Andrés was fifty-four years old, a husband, a father of two grown children, and the owner of a small construction company in Houston. For most of his adult life, he had seen himself as someone who could handle anything. That belief was forged in the crucible of his early thirties, when he spent eighteen months as a relief worker in a war-torn region of Central America. He had gone there to help rebuild schools and water systems, driven by a faith that hard work and good intentions could make a difference. Then came the afternoon he never spoke about afterward. He was in a village clinic, helping unload supplies, when a firefight erupted outside. He heard the sharp, percussive crack of a gunshot-so close it seemed to split the air beside his ear-and then the man next to him, a local nurse, crumpled to the ground. Andrés had been close enough to feel the spray of blood on his own face. He had frozen, unable to move, as the world narrowed to that single sound and the sudden, impossible stillness of the man at his feet. He did not remember how he got out. He only remembered the silence afterward, and the way his hands shook for days.

For years, Andrés told himself he had moved on. He built his business, raised his children, and kept his wife close. But in the last year, something had begun to fray. It started with a sound. A car backfiring in a parking lot would drop him into a cold sweat, his heart thudding so hard he felt dizzy. He would find himself scanning the faces around him, looking for threats, unable to shake the certainty that violence was about to erupt. He began to carry a weapon-a small handgun he kept in his truck or on his hip beneath his jacket-telling himself it was just sensible preparation. He told his wife it was for the construction sites, for the occasional rough neighborhood. But he knew the truth: the gun was a way to feel less helpless, a way to push back against the memory of that frozen moment when he had done nothing.

The triggers kept multiplying. Physical proximity became unbearable. In the grocery store, if someone stood too close in line, his jaw would clench and he would step away, his mind racing with images of a crowded clinic and a man falling. He began to avoid crowds entirely, delegating supply runs to his foreman. But the worst trigger, the one that confused him most, was positive emotion. He would be sitting at dinner with his wife, laughing at something she said, and suddenly a wave of wrongness would wash over him-a feeling that he did not deserve this, that joy was a betrayal of the dead. The laughter would die in his throat, and he would grow quiet, and his wife would ask what was wrong, and he would say nothing.

To escape that feeling, Andrés had developed a pattern he did not fully recognize as a pattern. He would pick arguments. Small ones, at first-a complaint about the way she loaded the dishwasher, a sharp comment about a bill. Then bigger ones, at the job site, with subcontractors who were late or careless. The arguments gave him something to focus on, a surge of adrenaline that drowned out the quieter, more dangerous feelings of shame and helplessness. He would go over and over the event in his head, replaying the gunshot, the fall, his own paralysis, asking himself why it had happened to him and not to someone else, as if an answer might release him. But the rumination only made the triggers more vivid. The more he thought about that day, the more he heard the gunshot in every loud noise, the more he felt the threat in every close space.

The cycle tightened. The arguments he started would leave him feeling raw and guilty, and then the guilt would feed the rumination, and the rumination would sharpen the triggers, and the triggers would drive him back to the gun, back to the conflicts, back to the same weary loop. His wife had begun to sleep in the guest room. His foreman had told him, gently, that the crew was getting nervous. Andrés had come to believe that he was losing control of everything he had built-his business, his marriage, his sense of himself as a good man.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in his own living room. His daughter had come for Sunday dinner, and she had brought her new boyfriend. Andrés had liked the young man immediately, had felt a warmth and a pride in seeing his daughter happy. And then, without warning, the warmth curdled into something else-a tightness in his chest, a sense that this happiness was borrowed, that it would be taken away. He had excused himself and gone to the garage, where he sat in his truck with the gun in the glovebox, and he had wept. He did not know what he was afraid of, exactly. He only knew he could not keep living this way. He wanted to stop carrying the weight of that afternoon, to feel something other than the constant vigilance and the hollow guilt. He wanted to laugh at dinner again, and mean it.
